reason: A scutellum (grass embryo or lichen disc) is not described as spreading. The pair most likely comes from the wrong part being matched.
'Spur' here is a floral or petal spur or a leaf-like margin, not a short shoot. The pair exists only through a wrong reading of the part.
Bracteoles can be ascending.
The examples describe an annular scar or node on the fruit. The scar is ring-shaped, not the fruit.
Achenes can be clavate, and the examples are correct.
Pedicel counts per umbellet are a normal counted-part case.
The part is unnamed, and the examples (narrowed to the apex or the throat) are about a tube or throat of a different part. A rule would need the bearer to be a tubular or lobed organ.
The examples mix 'acute' (a tip shape) with 'apiculate'. These should map to the apex shape, not the sharpness attribute. A rule would need to tell the tip shape from the sharpness.
A standard petal can be sericeous.
Samaras can be pubescent. One example is about the stigmatic surface, but the pair is fine.
Globose traps are spherical, so the pair is meaningful.
Ligulate or strap-shaped lobes are normal.
Small glands are a normal size statement.
Counts of cyathia per cyme are a counted-part case.
In mosses an operculum is either differentiated or not from the capsule. This is a correct use.
Pseudoparaphyllia can be present or absent.
A leaf apex can be rough or roughened.
A leaf apex or acumen can be broad.
A calyptra base can be entire, since the margin is entire.
'Evenly foliate' is about how leaves are arranged, not about a structure quality of the shoot system. The generic PATO structure term is the wrong reading.
Veins are sunken on the upper side of a leaf, and the examples are correct.
A height measurement of a part, such as a leaf scar, is meaningful.
A lamina margin can be crenate or crenulate (scalloped). The margin would be the better bearer, but the pair is meaningful.
Leaves can be coloured, for example by anthocyanin.
Seedlings can be hairy, puberulent or glabrescent.
Stipules are caducous, fugacious or persistent, which is a duration.
Pappus elements (bristles) can be ciliate.
The examples say the veins are joined or confluent, a connection between veins. The generic structure term is the wrong reading.
A cyme can be dense.
A keel petal has a length.
Slender lobes and teeth are meaningful.
Domatia can be glabrous.
Chains and hairs can be branched or forked.
The examples are about the stigmatic zone running longitudinally, not the stigma's own orientation. A rule would need to take the stigmatic zone as the bearer.
Parts can be broad, and a width in mm is also fine.
Lobes and similar parts can be obovate.
Pseudobulbs and stems can be four-angled.
A flower has a width.
Drupelets can be large.
An androphore can be narrow.
Domatia are described by position, such as axillary.
A hypanthium narrows into a neck, so it can be tapered.
Petiolules can be terete.
The examples are hyaline cells and leaf margins, not hairs on the shoot axis. The part is wrong.
Sap can be present or absent.
A staminal disc can be flat.
'Subentire' is a margin shape. It is read as 'unstructured', and the part is wrong.
Colour is meaningful for the part.
A sepal can be trumpet-shaped. 'Bucciniform' is a close match.
Spine-shields can be oblong.
The dendritic or stellate hairs belong to the trichomes, not the branch. 'Dendroid' for a branch means tree-like, which is a different meaning.
A keel petal can be arcuate or curved.
Trichomes can be retrorse.
The examples describe the margins of stigma or style lobes or the crown, not the ovary. The ovary wall is not described as entire.
The examples describe a toothed apex or crown margin, which belongs to another part. An ovary is not dentate.
The height of a pappus crown is meaningful.
A leaf base can be broadened.
Leaves are semi-evergreen or semi-deciduous.
Appendages and lobes can be ovate.
Corona lobes and filaments can be long.
